title: John's head (Mark 6:14–29)
hookLine: a drunken promise at a party and the death of the Baptist, told in flashback
last: LESS IN THE BAG, MORE TRUST.

cards: While the twelve are out in the villages, the news reaches the palace. Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, hears what's being done in Jesus's name.
People are guessing who Jesus is: Elijah come back, one of the old prophets. Herod has his own answer, and it's a guilty one. It's John, he says, the one I beheaded.
He's risen. Then Mark stops the story and flashes back, to tell how John the Baptist died.

teach.b: Herod had married Herodias, who had been married to his brother. John told him to his face that it wasn't lawful, so Herod had him chained in prison. But here's Mark's twist: Herod was fascinated by John.

He feared him, knew he was a good and holy man, and listened to him gladly, even though it left him troubled. Then comes Herod's birthday: a banquet for the officials, the officers, the leading men of Galilee.
The daughter of Herodias dances, and it pleases everyone.
And Herod, in front of all his guests, swears an open-ended promise, in the old King James Bible: "Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, I will give it thee, unto the half of my kingdom."
The girl goes out to her mother. What should I ask? The answer: the head of John the Baptist.

teach.h: EXCEEDING SORRY, YET FOR HIS OATH.
teach.b: "And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her." He does it anyway, because backing down in front of the room would cost him face. It's done.
John's disciples come for the body and bury him. In the King James text, Mark never names the girl.

teach.h: THE NAME SALOME IS FROM JOSEPHUS.
teach.b: The name Salome comes from the historian Josephus, who lists Herodias's daughter but doesn't tell this story. Mark doesn't say Herod was drunk either, only that it was a feast.
But the scene has the feel of it: a big promise, made to impress, and one man too proud to take it back. That closes a week: Legion. Go home and tell.
The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter.

how: Christians honor John the Baptist as a prophet who died for speaking the truth; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember his beheading with a feast on August 29.

o: a vision of John that Herod saw in a dream
what a ruler's careless oath at a feast cost
the reward Herod offered for finding Jesus

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: feared John and heard him gladly
danced, then asked for his head

s: the Gospel of Mark names the dancing girl Salome
the King James text of Mark doesn't name her. the name Salome comes from the historian Josephus.
Herod was exceeding sorry, but kept his oath anyway
for his oath's sake, and for the guests at the table.
Herod hated John and never listened to him
Mark says he feared him, knew he was holy, and heard him gladly.

games.q: you're Herod. in front of all your guests, you swore to give the girl anything. she asks for the head of a man you respect. what do you do?
o: break the oath in front of everyone.
keep the oath, though you're sorry.
offer her half the kingdom instead.
games.why: he was exceeding sorry, yet for his oath's sake, and for his guests, he would not refuse her.

practice: Think of promises you've made lately, I'll call you back, I'll fix it this weekend, and notice any made to look good or to end a conversation.

Choose one that matters to someone, one you've let slide, and picture keeping it; if you pray, ask for help to keep your word. If a promise was careless, it's all right to admit it and make a better one.

wordCard.voice: John's head. The price of a ruler's reckless oath at a feast, told by Mark as a flashback.

orig.note: Greek: an oath, a sworn promise. Herod kept his for the oath's sake.

carryVoice: Your line: careless words cost lives. A promise made to impress can cost more than it's worth. Half a year of days, and here you are.
